title: Worst headache of her life
presenting_complaint: Sudden, severe occipital headache that developed while at the gym 2 hours ago and peaked within a minute — "like being hit with a bat". She vomited twice.
history: No loss of consciousness, no seizure, no head trauma. Past medical history: hypertension, poorly controlled, on amlodipine. Smokes. Mother died of a "brain bleed" at 52. Not on anticoagulants or antiplatelets.

findings.name: Neurological examination
findings.value: GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, no focal neurological deficit

findings.name: Meningeal signs
findings.value: Photophobia present, neck stiffness present, Kernig sign negative

findings.name: Non-contrast head CT (2 hours from onset)
findings.value: Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and the Sylvian fissures

findings.name: CT angiography
findings.value: 7 mm aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery

diagnosis_options.label: Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm
diagnosis_options.explanation: Thunderclap occipital headache peaking within a minute, vomiting, meningism and photophobia, together with hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures on non-contrast CT and a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm on CT angiography, confirm a ruptured aneurysm causing subarachnoid haemorrhage.

diagnosis_options.label: Migraine
diagnosis_options.explanation: Migraine can cause severe headache with photophobia and vomiting, but it does not explain the sudden thunderclap onset, the meningism or the subarachnoid blood on CT.

diagnosis_options.label: Bacterial meningitis
diagnosis_options.explanation: Feverless meningism with a normal temperature of 37.4 °C, no infectious syndrome and subarachnoid blood on CT makes bacterial meningitis incorrect as the primary diagnosis.

diagnosis_options.label: Hypertensive encephalopathy
diagnosis_options.explanation: Blood pressure is elevated but there is no encephalopathy (GCS 15, no focal deficit, no papilloedema), and the CT findings point to subarachnoid haemorrhage rather than hypertensive encephalopathy.

diagnosis_options.label: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
diagnosis_options.explanation: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome can present with thunderclap headache, but here CT shows subarachnoid blood and CT angiography shows a discrete saccular aneurysm, not diffuse segmental vasoconstriction.

management_options.label: Urgent neurosurgical / neurointerventional referral for aneurysm securing (coiling or clipping)
management_options.explanation: Securing the ruptured aneurysm is the essential definitive treatment to prevent rebleeding.

management_options.label: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours
management_options.explanation: Nimodipine is indicated to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia due to vasospasm after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.

management_options.label: Control systolic blood pressure below 160 mmHg with a titratable IV agent
management_options.explanation: Blood pressure control reduces the risk of rebleeding from the unsecured aneurysm while avoiding excessive hypotension that could worsen cerebral perfusion.

management_options.label: Analgesia and antiemetic
management_options.explanation: Symptomatic treatment of headache and vomiting is reasonable but not the essential management of the underlying haemorrhage.

management_options.label: Lumbar puncture now
management_options.explanation: Lumbar puncture is not needed after a diagnostic CT showing subarachnoid haemorrhage and carries a risk of provoking rebleeding.

management_options.label: Aspirin
management_options.explanation: Antiplatelet therapy is harmful in an unsecured ruptured aneurysm because it increases the risk of rebleeding.
